The great voice, which we might have called disembodied, so impossible was it to connect it with any machinery of keys or pipes, hushed its resonant notes. The girl turned to assist her elderly companion and at last caught sight of us.

He was her father, and from her earliest years she had directed his sightless footsteps. They were Saxon Germans who had emigrated only a few years earlier and established fresh attachments among the neighbouring villagers. Near the outbreak of the pestilence, a young German student had come to join them. Their little history was readily guessed. Of noble birth, he loved the poor musician's beautiful daughter and had followed them when they fled his friends' persecution. But soon the great leveller advanced with its scythe still sharp, cutting down the field's lofty flowers along with its grass. The young man was among the first to perish. She kept herself alive for her father's sake. His blindness enabled her to maintain an illusion born initially of chance; and now, though they were solitary creatures, the country's only survivors, he knew nothing of the alteration. He did not understand that, when he heard his daughter play, only the silent mountains, insensible lake, and unknowing trees listened besides himself.

On the very day of our coming, she had fallen ill with the dreaded symptoms. The prospect of abandoning her old, blind father upon an unpeopled earth froze her with terror. Yet she lacked the courage to reveal the truth, and the extremity of her despair gave her strength for extraordinary efforts. At the usual hour for vespers she conducted him to the chapel. Though she shook and wept for his sake, she played, without a mistaken note or faltering measure, the hymn honouring the creation of the beautiful earth that would soon receive her body.

Our arrival seemed to her a visitation from heaven. At the first appearance of help, her fiercely summoned courage and barely maintained resolution deserted her. Crying out, she ran toward us, clasped Adrian's knees, and with only the words, “Oh, save my father!” released in sobs and frantic cries the long-restrained torrent of her grief.

Unhappy girl! She and her father lie together now beneath the tall walnut that shelters her lover, the tree she indicated to us while dying. Her father, finally understanding her peril but unable to witness the changes in that beloved face, clung stubbornly to her hand until death had made it cold and rigid. Still he neither stirred nor spoke, until, twelve hours later, merciful death admitted him to unbroken rest. Beneath the turf they sleep, with the tree for their memorial. I remember that sacred place distinctly, enclosed by rugged Jura and the remote, boundless Alps. The church spire still rises among its sheltering trees; and though her hand is cold, I fancy that the heavenly music they cherished yet drifts around them, comforting their gentle spirits.

As they were leaving the dining-room, the tower clock began its booming announcement of midnight. With the final stroke came a crash and a sharp, sudden cry. A fearful clap of thunder rattled the house; a phrase of otherworldly music drifted on the air; and a panel above the stairs burst open with a loud report. Onto the landing stepped Virginia, exceedingly pale, carrying a small casket. Instantly they all hurried up to her. Mrs. Otis caught her in a fervent embrace, the Duke overwhelmed her with ardent kisses, and the twins performed a frantic war-dance about them.

“Good heavens, child! Where have you been?” demanded Mr. Otis, somewhat angrily, suspecting her of having played a foolish prank upon them. “Cecil and I have ridden all over the countryside in search of you, and your mother has been nearly frightened to death. You must never attempt such practical jokes again.”

“Unless they're on the Ghost! Unless they're on the Ghost!” cried the twins, leaping about.

“My darling girl, thank God we have you back. You must never go away from me again,” whispered Mrs. Otis, kissing the shaking child and smoothing her tangled golden hair.

“Papa,” Virginia said softly, “I have been with the Ghost. He has died, and you must come to see him. He had done very wicked things, but he was truly sorry for them all, and before he died he gave me this box of lovely jewels.”

Her family regarded her with speechless astonishment, but her manner was entirely sober and earnest. Turning, she guided them through the gap in the wood panelling and along a narrow hidden passage. Washington followed with a burning candle he had snatched from the table. At length they reached a massive oak door set with rusted nails. It swung inward on its weighty hinges at Virginia's touch, admitting them to a small, low chamber with a vaulted roof and a single tiny barred window. A large iron ring was fixed in the wall, and to it was chained a gaunt skeleton, lying at full length upon the stone floor. Its long, bare fingers appeared to reach for an old-fashioned platter and water jug placed barely beyond their grasp. The jug must once have contained water, for green mould coated its interior. Upon the platter lay nothing but a heap of dust. Virginia knelt beside the skeleton, joined her small hands, and prayed without a sound. The others watched in amazement as the secret of that dreadful tragedy lay revealed before them.

You've encouraged an artificial soul and spirit in him, ma'am, quite unbefitting his station: as the board, Mrs. Sowerberry, being practical philosophers, will assure you. What concern have paupers with souls or spirits? It's enough that we permit them to keep their bodies alive. Had you fed the boy on gruel, ma'am, this never would have occurred.”

“Dear me, dear me!” cried Mrs. Sowerberry, lifting her gaze devoutly towards the kitchen ceiling. “Such are the consequences of liberality!”

Mrs. Sowerberry's liberality towards Oliver had amounted to bestowing upon him a plentiful supply of the dirty remnants that no one else would touch. It therefore argued much meekness and devotion to others that she willingly submitted to Mr. Bumble's weighty charge, of which, in fairness to her, she was utterly guiltless in thought, speech, or deed.

“Ah!” observed Mr. Bumble, once the lady's gaze had returned to earthly things, “the only remedy I know is to keep him in the cellar a day or two, till he's somewhat reduced by hunger; then bring him out and put him on gruel for the whole term of his apprenticeship. His family is a bad one. Excitable dispositions, Mrs. Sowerberry! The doctor and nurse both declared that his mother reached this place through hardships and suffering which would have finished any well-disposed woman weeks before.”

At this stage of Mr. Bumble's address, Oliver, catching enough to understand that his mother had been mentioned, began kicking afresh with such force that no other sound could be heard. At that moment Sowerberry came back. The ladies acquainted him with Oliver's crime, supplying those embellishments they considered most likely to kindle his wrath; whereupon he unlocked the cellar in an instant and pulled his mutinous apprentice out by his collar.

The beating had left Oliver's clothes torn, his face scratched and bruised, and his hair disordered across his brow. Yet the flush of anger remained; and on being dragged from confinement he frowned defiantly at Noah, showing himself wholly undaunted.

“A fine young gentleman you are, aren't you?” said Sowerberry, shaking Oliver and boxing his ear.

“He spoke against my mother,” answered Oliver.

“And supposing he did, you ungrateful little wretch?” said Mrs. Sowerberry. “She deserved his words, and worse besides.”

“No, she didn't,” said Oliver.

“Yes, she did,” Mrs. Sowerberry returned.

“It's false!” said Oliver.

Mrs. Sowerberry dissolved into a torrent of tears.

That torrent deprived Mr. Sowerberry of every alternative. Every reader of experience must plainly see that, had he delayed for a single moment to chastise Oliver with the utmost severity, all the settled precedents of matrimonial quarrels would have pronounced him a brute, an unnatural husband, an insulting being, a paltry counterfeit of a man, and a variety of other flattering characters too numerous to enumerate within this chapter's bounds.
